Series::minimum¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::minimum(const Series& rhs) const -> Series
Series::minimum(double rhs) const -> Series
Series& Series::minimum_(double rhs)

What It Does¶

minimum() compares two values position by position and keeps the smaller one at each broadcasted location.

This is the value-wise mirror of maximum, but the same usage idea applies: this is an elementwise comparison, not a reduction.

Use it when you want to:

  • merge two value sources by keeping the lower side

  • apply a shared ceiling

  • enforce per-lane upper limits through broadcasting

  • reason in terms of comparisons rather than in terms of a dedicated clamp call

Parameters¶

rhs (const Series& or double)

The right-hand operand.

When you call minimum(const Series& rhs):

  • rhs is broadcast against self

  • both sides are treated as ordinary value sources

  • the output shape is the broadcasted shape

  • the output dtype follows the two-operand rules for the two Series

When you call minimum(double rhs):

  • every element of self compares against one shared scalar

  • the scalar follows self’s execution path

  • the method often reads like “apply a ceiling,” but it is still a comparison operator

The everyday rule is:

  • use the Series overload when both sides are structured data

  • use the scalar overload when one side is a repeated ceiling-like value

Returns¶

Series A new Series containing the smaller value at each broadcasted position.

Gradient¶

minimum() is differentiable in both operands.

The backward rule is:

  • gradient flows to self where self <= rhs

  • gradient flows to rhs where self > rhs

The tie rule is intentionally the same as maximum(), not the opposite. That gives the comparison family one consistent boundary convention.

Note

Tie-breaking convention When self[i] == rhs[i], the full gradient still goes to self. The engine uses one consistent comparison-boundary convention across maximum()/minimum()/clamp_min()/clamp_max() rather than flipping the tie direction between max-like and min-like operations.

In-Place Form¶

minimum_() is the in-place sibling of minimum(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 5.0, 3.0}, {3});
x.minimum_(4.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 4, 3]

Examples¶

The examples below build from the ordinary broadcast case through scalar ceiling behavior and the tie rule that matters in autodiff code.

Example 1. A row-shaped peer broadcasts across the leading dimension.

auto grid = pluss::make_series({1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 8},
    {2, 3});
auto peer = pluss::make_series({2, 6, 1}, {3});

std::cout << grid.minimum(peer);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 5, 1],
  [2, 2, 1]]

This is the same broadcast pattern as maximum, but each location keeps the smaller side instead of the larger one.

Example 2. A column-shaped peer broadcasts across the trailing dimension.

auto column_peer = pluss::make_series({2, 6}, {2, 1});

std::cout << grid.minimum(column_peer);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 2, 2],
  [4, 2, 6]]

This example is worth studying because it shows how much the broadcast pattern matters:

  • row 0 compares against 2

  • row 1 compares against 6

Example 3. The scalar overload caps every element against one shared ceiling.

std::cout << grid.minimum(4.5);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 4.5, 3],
  [4, 2, 4.5]]

Only positions above 4.5 are pulled down. This is the same numerical idea as clamp_max, but expressed as an ordinary binary comparison.

Example 4. On an integer Series, the scalar overload stays on the integer path.

auto int_grid = pluss::make_series({1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 8},
    {2, 3});

std::cout << int_grid.minimum(4.5);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=int32, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 4, 3],
  [4, 2, 4]]

This verified result shows the same quirk as maximum():

  • the output remains int32

  • the scalar does not force a floating destination

  • if fractional ceilings matter, start from a floating Series

Example 5. The tie still attributes its derivative to self.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1, 5, 2}, {3});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4, 2, 2}, {3});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = a.minimum(b);
y.sum().reverse();
std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 2]
da=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 1]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 0]

Index 2 is again the decisive boundary case:

  • both operands are 2

  • the forward result is therefore 2

  • only a receives the derivative because the tie belongs to self

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • minimum() is non-mutating. The inputs are left unchanged.

  • Broadcast compatibility still applies. If the two operands cannot broadcast to one shared shape, the call fails.

  • The scalar overload follows the left-hand Series path. On integer input, the verified behavior stays integer.

  • minimum() is not a reduction. If you want an axis-wise or global smallest value, use min.

  • If the scalar is conceptually acting as an upper bound, clamp_max may express intent more directly.

Summary¶

Read minimum() in one of two ways:

  • Series overload: “pick the smaller source at each position”

  • scalar overload: “do not let any value rise above this ceiling”

See Also¶

  • Series::maximum: the larger-side counterpart.

  • Series::clamp_max: one-sided upper bound with the same inclusive comparison boundary.

  • Series::clamp_min: one-sided lower bound from the same comparison family.
